introduction-the-field-of-dreams-fallacy.core: 'If you build it, they will come' fails for platforms. Developers adopt what solves their problems, so the platform has to be built and run like a product, with users, research, a roadmap, marketing and metrics.

first_principles.problem: A platform team spends a year building an elaborate platform that few teams adopt, because it solved problems nobody had.
truths: Adoption is voluntary in healthy organisations.
Builders' assumptions often differ from users' needs.

analogy.title: A baseball diamond in a cornfield
analogy.story: In the film the players came; in real organisations, nobody comes unless the field meets a real need.
analogy.breaks: Some capabilities (security baselines) may be mandatory, but even those need good UX.

example.title: Two platform launches
flow: Team B: interviews → TVP in 6 weeks → 60% adoption, iterate

check.q: What's the 'Field of Dreams' fallacy in platform engineering?
check.a: Assuming developers will adopt a platform just because it exists, without validating that it solves their needs.

platform-as-a-product-the-value-proposit.core: An Internal Developer Platform is a curated set of self-service capabilities (deploy, provision, observe, secure) that lets product teams deliver faster with less cognitive load. Its value proposition is speed, safety and focus.

first_principles.problem: Platform teams describe their work as 'Kubernetes and Terraform modules' rather than value developers care about.
truths: Developers care about outcomes, not tools.
derivation: Define the **value proposition** in developer terms (ship in minutes, safely).

analogy.title: A meal kit service
analogy.story: You don't want to source ingredients; you want a great dinner with minimal effort, and the kit is curated for that.
analogy.breaks: Over-curation limits flexibility, so offer escape hatches.

example.title: Reframing platform features
flow: Before: 'We run EKS with ArgoCD and Vault'
After: 'Get a production-ready service with CI/CD, secrets and dashboards in 10 minutes'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Developers understand why they should care.

check.q: How should a platform's value be expressed?
check.a: In developer outcomes, such as how quickly and safely they can ship, rather than in the tools used.

the-core-driver-cognitive-load.core: The deeper reason for a platform is reducing cognitive load. Developers can't be experts in their domain and also in Kubernetes, IAM, networking and observability, so the platform absorbs that extraneous load.

first_principles.problem: Product engineers spend half their time wrestling with infrastructure instead of building features.

analogy.title: Driving an automatic vs. a manual car with no dashboard
analogy.story: Hide the gear changes, show the essential gauges, and let the driver focus on the road.
analogy.breaks: Hiding too much prevents debugging, so make abstractions transparent when needed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: More business value from the same team.

check.q: What type of cognitive load should a platform absorb?
check.a: Extraneous load: infrastructure and tooling complexity unrelated to the team's domain.

user-research-knowing-your-customer.core: Validate rather than guess: interview developers, shadow their workflows, run surveys and analyse support tickets to find the real pain points before building. Platform engineers aren't typical users.

first_principles.problem: The platform team builds a sophisticated service mesh UI while developers' biggest pain is a 40-minute CI wait.
truths: Builders' needs differ from users' needs.
derivation: **Interview** a range of developers (new, senior, different stacks).

analogy.title: A doctor taking a history before prescribing
analogy.story: Asking about symptoms beats guessing a diagnosis.
analogy.breaks: Users ask for solutions ('faster horses'), so dig for the underlying problem.

example.title: A research sprint
flow: Top pain: environment setup takes 2 days

check.q: Why shadow developers rather than only asking them what they want?
check.a: Observed behaviour reveals real pain and workarounds that people don't think to mention.

roadmapping-sharing-the-vision.core: Replace multi-year Gantt charts with outcome-based roadmaps (Now / Next / Later, themes tied to developer outcomes) that are shared publicly and updated with feedback, so users know what's coming and can influence it.

first_principles.problem: Developers don't know what the platform team is working on, so they build their own workarounds.

analogy.title: A restaurant's 'coming soon' menu board
analogy.story: Diners know what's planned, can request favourites, and don't open their own kitchens.
analogy.breaks: Roadmaps aren't promises, so communicate the uncertainty for 'Later' items.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Teams wait for or shape features instead of building their own.

check.q: Why use Now/Next/Later instead of a detailed Gantt chart?
check.a: It communicates direction and priorities while being honest about uncertainty, and adapts as you learn.

thinnest-viable-platform-tvp.core: Don't build the Death Star. Start with the Thinnest Viable Platform, the smallest set of capabilities that solves real pain (sometimes just a wiki page of standards plus a template), then grow it based on usage and feedback.

first_principles.problem: Teams spend 18 months on a comprehensive platform that's outdated or mismatched by launch.
truths: Simple solutions are faster to adopt.
derivation: Build the **minimum** that solves it (docs, a template, a script).
**Iterate** and add only what proves its value.

analogy.title: Building a bridge one plank at a time
analogy.story: A simple footbridge gets people across now; widen it once you know traffic patterns.
analogy.breaks: Too thin can mean too fragile, so ensure reliability for whatever you ship.

example.title: A TVP evolution
flow: Month 1: wiki of standards + service template
example.outcome: platforms that grow from proven value.

check.q: What is a Thinnest Viable Platform?
check.a: The smallest set of platform capabilities, possibly just docs and templates, that solves real developer pain, grown incrementally from there.

adoption-curves-crossing-the-internal-ch.core: Internal adoption follows the technology adoption curve: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards. The 'chasm' between early adopters and the pragmatic majority is crossed with proven references, polish and migration support.

first_principles.problem: A few enthusiastic teams adopt the platform, then adoption stalls because mainstream teams need proof and ease.
derivation: **Polish** the docs, defaults and support for the majority.
**Provide migration help**, and use **deprecation** for laggards.

analogy.title: Smartphone adoption
analogy.story: Tech enthusiasts first, then mainstream users once apps, reliability and friends' recommendations arrived.
analogy.breaks: Forcing adoption too early backfires, so earn the majority.

example.title: Crossing the chasm
flow: Early majority adopts; 70% in a year

check.q: What helps a platform cross from early adopters to the majority?
check.a: Proven success stories, polished docs and defaults, and hands-on migration support.

marketing-the-platform-internal-devrel.core: Since adoption is voluntary, sell the platform: demos, newsletters, office hours, champions in product teams, internal case studies and great docs. Internal DevRel builds awareness, trust and a feedback loop.

first_principles.problem: A useful platform capability goes unused because nobody knows it exists.

analogy.title: A product launch campaign
analogy.story: Even great products need announcements, demos and testimonials.
analogy.breaks: Marketing can't fix a bad product. Quality comes first.

example.title: A quarterly platform update
example.outcome: developers know about, and trust, the platform.

check.q: Why does a platform team need internal marketing?
check.a: Voluntary adoption depends on awareness and trust, which great features alone don't create.

measuring-success-key-metrics.core: Product metrics for platforms: adoption (teams or services onboarded), engagement (active usage), satisfaction (NPS, CSAT), time-to-value (time to first deploy), and outcome metrics (DORA, cognitive load), so investment can be guided.

first_principles.problem: The platform team can't show whether its work makes any difference, so funding is at risk.
derivation: **Outcomes**: DORA metrics, time spent on infra.

analogy.title: A SaaS company's product dashboard
analogy.story: Signups, active users, NPS and churn tell you if the product is working.
analogy.breaks: Vanity metrics (number of features) mislead, so focus on outcomes.

example.title: A platform scorecard
flow: Time to first deploy: 2 days → 2 hours

check.q: Name two key product metrics for an internal platform.
check.a: For example, the adoption rate of golden paths and developer satisfaction (NPS), plus time-to-value.
